title: Birth Companions’ Lived Experiences During Childbirth: Implications for Professional Nursing Practice
content: Background/Objectives: The presence of a support person during childbirth has demonstrated positive maternal and neonatal effects; however, the lived experience of these individuals has been less explored. The aim of this study was to explore the lived experiences of birth companions during childbirth, including their perceived barriers, interactions with health care providers, and opportunities for improving maternity care. Methods: A qualitative phenomenological study guided by Van Manen’s methodological perspective was conducted in a tertiary university hospital. In-depth interviews were conducted with 18 birth companions who provided continuous support throughout childbirth. Interviews were recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using inductive thematic analysis supported by ATLAS.ti and complemented by co-occurrence analysis. Investigator triangulation, participant review, and reflexive strategies enhanced trustworthiness. Results: Analysis identified one overarching meta-theme, The childbirth accompaniment experience, encompassing four themes: Emotional experience, Experiencing Childbirth as a companion, Interactions with health care providers, and Physical care environment. Participants described childbirth as a meaningful and predominantly positive experience characterized by profound emotional connection, strengthened family bonding, and active involvement in supporting the woman. However, communication barriers, limited participation in certain aspects of care, organizational practices, and the physical environment diminished feelings of inclusion and comfort. Conclusions: Recognizing birth companions as active participants, strengthening clinical communication, promoting inclusive practices, and adapting the physical environment may facilitate their participation and contribute to more supportive, compassionate, and person-centered maternity care.
